sections.name: Background
texts: I'm Radostina, a Management and Business Information Systems student at the Technical University of Sofia. Most days I'm somewhere between a spreadsheet and a sketchbook — one week deep in database normalization and SWOT analysis, the next lost in a UI design system or a half-finished painting.

Studying business alongside design gave me a slightly different instinct than most designers pick up. I don't only ask whether something looks right — I ask whether it works, whether it scales, whether the logic underneath actually holds. That habit doesn't stay in the classroom. It shows up in how I plan a recipe, structure a painting, or figure out why a half-formed idea isn't coming together yet.

sections.name: Hero
texts: Design student, business student, painter, occasional baker — most of it comes down to the same instinct: take something that could be beautiful, and make sure it also works.

sections.name: what i've learned
texts: A new, structured approach to user research, prototyping, and user testing.
A strong understanding of industry standards, UX principles, and design techniques.

The importance of collaboration and iteration in the product design process — how to gather user feedback, incorporate it into my designs, and continuously improve the product based on real user needs and preferences.

sections.name: search
texts: Dog walker search. Schedule a walk.

During the user testing phase, I conducted usability tests focused on the dog walker search and booking flow. The main tasks included browsing available dog walkers, evaluating how users perceive trust through profiles, ratings, and reviews, and scheduling a walk with a selected walker. The testing revealed a key usability issue related to availability clarity — users found it difficult to quickly identify free dates in the calendar. Based on this feedback, I will improved the calendar design in the future by making available and unavailable dates more visually distinct.
Overall, users described the search experience as intuitive and engaging, and the improved scheduling flow will help reduce friction during the booking process even more.
The average time for users to schedule a walk with a chosen walker

sections.name: onboarding
texts: During the user testing phase, I evaluated the core onboarding experience of the app, with a focus on the sign-up flow and pet profile creation. Participants were asked to complete key tasks such as creating an account and adding their pet’s details. By observing user behavior and collecting qualitative feedback, I assessed how intuitive and accessible these essential features were.

The testing revealed mostly positive results, as users found the app easy to navigate and the processes clear and straightforward. The insights gathered helped identify minor usability improvements and validated the overall structure of the onboarding flow.
The average time for users to sign up and complete the pet profile.

sections.name: the problem
texts: What is the problem we are trying to solve?

Busy urban dog owners often struggle to find reliable dog walkers at the right time and location. Existing solutions can be confusing or overwhelming, making it difficult to book services efficiently. The goal of this project was to design an app that simplifies the process, allowing users to find and book dog walkers quickly, while reducing cognitive load and providing clear information about availability and location.

sections.name: design brief
texts:
1. UX Design
To begin this project, I conducted user research in order to better understand dog owners’ needs, behaviors, and pain points. This included desk research, competitor analysis, and user interviews. Based on the findings, I created a user persona and defined the main problems to be solved. Additionally, I designed a user flow that visually represents the journey of a dog owner from discovering the app to booking a dog walk.

2. UI Design
With the target users in mind, I designed the visual direction of the app. This phase included creating wireframes and defining the overall look and feel of the interface. The focus was on clarity, friendliness, and trust, using simple layouts, clear typography, and a consistent color palette to support an intuitive user experience.

3. Interaction
Following the UI phase, I developed an interactive prototype in Figma. The prototype demonstrates the core user flows of the app, including sign-up, browsing dog walkers, and scheduling a dog walk. The goal of this phase was to ensure smooth interactions and logical transitions between screens.

4. User Testing
In the final phase, I conducted usability testing on the interactive prototype. The objective was to evaluate the overall user experience, validate design decisions, and identify areas that could be improved.

sections.name: conclusions
texts: Building a two-layer token system (primitives → semantic aliases) makes color changes trivial — updating one value updates every component that uses it.
Component properties (boolean, enum, instance swap) are far more powerful than duplicating frames — the session list item covers 5 states from a single component.
Documenting UI patterns forces clarity — writing the "don't" rules revealed design decisions I hadn't consciously made.
Define the token system before building any components — retrofitting semantic aliases is slower than designing them in from the start.
Build a stronger illustration language earlier — the visual language of blobs and ambient shapes emerged gradually rather than being defined upfront.

sections.name: Accessibility
texts: Minimum contrast ratio 4.5:1 for normal text · 3:1 for large text and UI components
All functionality operable via keyboard · no keyboard traps outside intentional dialogs
Text resizes up to 200% without loss of content or functionality
Dark text on violet-800 and stone-900 achieves enhanced contrast above 7:1

sections.name: breakpoints
texts: hamburger drawer · stacked panels · bottom nav
full-width stack · search inline · CTA in content

The RWD strategy followed one core principle: the same components, reorganised rather than redesigned. The session list item looks identical at every breakpoint — what changes is the container it sits in. On desktop, panels sit side by side in a two-column grid. On tablet, they stack. On mobile, the stat cards become horizontally scrollable rather than cramming into a fixed three-column grid. These are layout decisions, not component decisions, which is exactly how a well-built design system should behave.

The navigation change was the most significant breakpoint decision: a persistent sidebar on desktop, a hamburger drawer on tablet, and a bottom tab bar on mobile. This isn't just a size adaptation — it's a fundamentally different interaction pattern driven by the input method. Desktop users navigate with a mouse and have horizontal space to spare. Mobile users navigate with their thumb and need the most-used actions within reach at the bottom of the screen.

sections.name: screens
texts:
I designed the screens in user journey order rather than by complexity, which helped me make consistent decisions. The landing page needed to do three things: communicate what the product is, create emotional desire, and reduce friction to sign up. The floating UI cards showing the session player and mood chart were a deliberate choice — rather than generic marketing copy, I showed the actual product, which is both more honest and more persuasive.

The empty dashboard was one of the more interesting design challenges. Most first-time users arrive with no sessions, no mood data, and no streak — so the dashboard risks looking broken or unfinished. I solved this with a three-step onboarding checklist that makes the empty state feel like the beginning of something rather than the absence of something.

sections.name: patterns
texts: Show only essential info by default. Reveal more when the user signals intent — mood check-in expands inline after tapping an icon.
Disclose next step after user commits
Hide info needed for a decision
When no content exists, show illustration + headline + single CTA. Never leave a blank area with no explanation.
One CTA — a clear next action
Premium sessions stay visible but dimmed + lock icon. Tapping opens a soft paywall sheet, not a blocking modal.
Keep items visible at low opacity

sections.name: Components
texts: Every component in Aura was built with one principle in mind: it should be impossible to use incorrectly. This is why the input field forces the label to always be visible above the field — it cannot be accidentally removed. It's why the button has a strict hierarchy (Primary / Secondary / Tertiary) with one Primary per section maximum — the system makes the correct choice the easiest choice. Building nested components — where the Session List Panel contains instances of the Session List Item — also taught me how design systems scale. A change to the Item component propagated instantly to every Panel on every screen. That felt like the difference between maintaining a product and maintaining a system.

sections.name: Typography
texts: The type scale uses a 1.25 ratio starting from a 16px base, which produces a harmonious progression without the dramatic size jumps of a 1.5 ratio. The choice of weight 400 regular throughout was deliberate — heavier type would have made the product feel more assertive and transactional, which is the opposite of what Aura needs. A light weight keeps the reading experience quiet and unhurried, even when the content is informational. I reserved weight 500 for headings and labels only, which creates hierarchy through weight contrast rather than size alone.
4px base unit · all spacing is a multiple of 4 · never arbitrary pixel values

sections.name: Color system
texts:
Purple and violet have long been associated with spirituality, calm, and introspection across many cultures, which made Violet the obvious primary brand color. I deliberately moved away from the generic blue palette that dominates wellness and productivity apps — Aura needed to feel distinctive, not familiar.

The secondary palette was chosen to extend that feeling rather than introduce contrast for its own sake. Sage green brings a botanical, grounded quality. Honey yellow and Cherry red serve purely functional roles as warning and error colors, but I made sure they stayed warm-toned rather than defaulting to traffic-light red and yellow, so they didn't jar against the overall palette.

sections.name: Brand identity
texts: The name Aura came from the idea of an invisible but felt presence — which is exactly what good mindfulness practice is. It doesn't demand attention; it creates a quiet space around you. Once the name was decided, the color system followed naturally.

sections.name: Intro
texts: Aura is a mindfulness and meditation web app designed as part of an advanced UI course. The project delivers a full design system — from primitive color tokens through to documented components, UI patterns, and responsive screens.
